patient.chief_complaint: Increasing frequency of stereotyped episodes of unresponsiveness with right-hand automatisms over the past three months, refractory to two antiepileptic drug regimens, presenting for inpatient epilepsy monitoring unit admission
patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Johnson is a 47-year-old right-handed African American man with a six-year history of focal epilepsy presenting for inpatient video-EEG monitoring as part of a surgical evaluation. His seizures began at age 41 with a stereotyped sequence: an intense rising sensation in his epigastrium and an overpowering sense of deja vu lasting 5 to 10 seconds, followed by loss of awareness and repetitive automatisms consisting of lip smacking and fumbling movements of his right hand. Postictal confusion typically lasts 10 to 20 minutes. His wife reports that during episodes he sometimes turns his head slowly to the right and makes chewing movements, and he has on two occasions secondarily generalized to bilateral tonic-clonic activity with tongue biting.

At the time of initial diagnosis six years ago, he was evaluated at an outside hospital where a standard-protocol MRI of the brain was reported as normal and a routine 30-minute EEG was described as 'mild diffuse slowing, no epileptiform discharges.' He was diagnosed with focal epilepsy of unknown etiology and started on levetiracetam, which was discontinued after three months due to severe irritability and depression. Oxcarbazepine was then started but caused symptomatic hyponatremia requiring discontinuation. His current regimen of lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily plus carbamazepine 400 mg twice daily was started 18 months ago and initially reduced seizure frequency from approximately weekly to two to three per month. Over the past three months, however, seizures have increased to approximately four to six per week despite confirmed adherence. He denies any recent changes in sleep, alcohol intake, illness, or new medications. His wife notes that some episodes resolve within 30 seconds while others last up to two minutes.

He was referred to our comprehensive epilepsy center after a neurology outpatient visit. At that visit, a repeat outpatient EEG reportedly showed 'bilateral temporal slowing, greater on the left, with intermittent left and right temporal sharp transients of uncertain significance.' This ambiguous finding, combined with ongoing breakthrough seizures, prompted referral for inpatient evaluation. The patient and his family are motivated to pursue surgical evaluation given the functional impact of his epilepsy on his teaching career and independence. He has not driven for four years. He is admitted to the epilepsy monitoring unit for long-term video-EEG, updated MRI epilepsy protocol, and further evaluation.

results.title: Side of Lesions Predicts Surgical Outcomes in Patients With Drug-Resistant Temporal Lobe Epilepsy Secondary to Focal Cortical Dysplasia Type IIIa
results.summary: In a cohort of 43 patients with drug-resistant TLE and FCD Type IIIa (hippocampal sclerosis coexisting with adjacent FCD Type I in the temporal neocortex), 76.7% achieved seizure freedom following anterior temporal lobectomy. Right-sided lesions independently predicted better surgical outcome. Complete resection of both the hippocampus and the neocortical FCD component was associated with improved outcome compared to hippocampectomy alone.

results.title: Occult focal cortical dysplasia may predict poor outcome of surgery for drug-resistant mesial temporal lobe epilepsy
results.summary: In 82 patients with drug-resistant MTLE due to hippocampal sclerosis who appeared non-lesional on standard MRI, dual pathology (HS coexisting with neocortical FCD) was found histologically in 40% and was the most significant negative predictor of seizure-free surgical outcome. Dedicated 3T epilepsy protocol MRI with thin-cut coronal sequences is essential to identify subtle neocortical lesions missed on standard protocols.

results.title: Drug-resistant epilepsy: Definition, prevalence, and impact on outcomes
results.summary: ILAE 2010 definition of drug-resistant epilepsy: failure of adequate trials of two tolerated, appropriately chosen, and used AED schedules. Approximately one-third of all epilepsy patients will become drug-resistant. Early surgical referral for eligible candidates improves long-term outcomes compared to continued medical management alone.

results.title: ILAE evidence-based guideline on initial monotherapy for epileptic seizures
results.summary: For focal epilepsy, first-line AEDs with level A/B evidence include carbamazepine, levetiracetam, oxcarbazepine, phenobarbital, phenytoin, and zonisamide. Lamotrigine and lacosamide are level C/D options. Enzyme-inducing AEDs (carbamazepine, phenytoin) reduce plasma levels of co-administered non-inducer AEDs including lamotrigine.

output.proposed: Current regimen: Lamotrigine 200 mg BID plus Carbamazepine 400 mg BID; considering addition of lacosamide or clobazam for breakthrough seizure control pending surgical evaluation
interactions: Carbamazepine (strong CYP3A4/UGT1A4 inducer) reduces lamotrigine plasma concentrations by approximately 40-70% through induction of UGT1A4-mediated glucuronidation. A lamotrigine level of 3.2 mcg/mL at 200 mg BID dosing is consistent with enzyme-induction by carbamazepine — this is a pharmacokinetic effect, not a sign of non-adherence.
Carbamazepine autoinduces its own metabolism (CYP3A4); the measured carbamazepine level of 9.8 mcg/mL is therapeutic.
Lacosamide (if added): minimal CYP interactions; no clinically significant pharmacokinetic interaction with carbamazepine or lamotrigine. Safe co-administration.
Clobazam (if added): metabolized by CYP3A4 (to N-desmethylclobazam, further by CYP2C19); carbamazepine may modestly reduce clobazam levels. Monitor for reduced efficacy.
warnings: The low-normal lamotrigine level (3.2 mcg/mL; reference 3.0-14.0 mcg/mL) is at the lower boundary of the therapeutic range and may represent sub-therapeutic exposure in this patient given the enzyme-inducing co-medication; dose increase may be considered but must be weighed against seizure monitoring requirements.
Carbamazepine is associated with hyponatremia — monitor sodium levels, particularly relevant given prior hyponatremia-driven discontinuation of oxcarbazepine.
Do not interpret the low-normal lamotrigine level as evidence of non-adherence without accounting for the enzyme-inducing effect of carbamazepine.

sequence_constraints.reason: Structural cause (dual pathology, HS + FCD) influences AED selection and surgical planning; MRI findings should inform drug-interaction considerations for the surgical workup phase.

critical_actions: Apply ILAE drug-resistance criteria (failure of ≥2 appropriately chosen and tolerated AED schedules at adequate doses) and refer to a comprehensive epilepsy surgery center.
Obtain 3T MRI with dedicated epilepsy protocol to detect subtle left temporal neocortical pathology (FCD) missed on prior 1.5T standard MRI — dual pathology has major surgical planning implications.
Perform prolonged inpatient video-EEG monitoring to capture habitual events, confirm left temporal ictal onset, and exclude independent right temporal foci before surgical planning.
Order interictal FDG-PET as part of the presurgical evaluation to characterize metabolic extent of the left temporal epileptogenic zone.
Order neuropsychological battery to lateralize verbal memory function and quantify risk of post-operative verbal memory decline (dominant hemisphere surgery).
Do not interpret normal prolactin (drawn 3 hours post-event) as evidence of non-epileptic events — prolactin is only diagnostically useful within 10-20 minutes of a convulsion.
Recognize that carbamazepine-induced reduction of lamotrigine levels explains the low-normal lamotrigine concentration — this is a pharmacokinetic interaction, not proof of non-adherence.
Counsel patient on absolute driving restriction and document in chart; consider occupational safety implications for return to classroom teaching.
contraindicated_actions: Do not diagnose PNES or attribute seizures to non-epileptic events on the basis of a normal prolactin drawn hours after an event.
Do not conclude bitemporal epilepsy based on bilateral temporal EEG slowing alone without capturing ictal events — right temporal polymorphic slowing is non-ictal and may be propagated.
Do not perform LP in the absence of clinical indication (no encephalitis features).
Do not continue indefinite AED escalation without surgical evaluation once drug-resistance criteria are met.
Do not plan surgical resection of the hippocampus alone if dual pathology (neocortical FCD component) is identified — incomplete resection of the FCD increases surgical failure risk.
key_reasoning_points: Drug-resistant left temporal epilepsy in this patient meets ILAE criteria (failure of levetiracetam, oxcarbazepine, and ongoing breakthrough on lamotrigine + carbamazepine); surgical evaluation is the standard of care.

The bilateral temporal EEG slowing on the outpatient study and independent right temporal polymorphic delta on initial inpatient EEG are the principal red herrings; video-EEG with 17 captured events establishes exclusive left temporal ictal onset.

Standard 1.5T MRI showed only HS; the subtle left temporal neocortical signal change suggesting FCD IIIa is only visible on 3T dedicated epilepsy protocol — failure to recognize dual pathology would lead to incomplete surgical resection and higher seizure recurrence risk.
Normal prolactin drawn 3 hours post-event has no diagnostic value and should not be interpreted as evidence against a recent seizure; the diagnostic window is 10-20 minutes post-convulsion.

Low-normal lamotrigine level reflects carbamazepine-induced UGT1A4 induction (40-70% lamotrigine concentration reduction), not non-adherence; the drug interaction result correctly identifies this pharmacokinetic mechanism.

Material-specific verbal memory deficit (CVLT-II T-scores 31-34) with preserved visual memory localizes dysfunction to the dominant left temporal lobe; neuropsych evaluation is critical for pre-surgical counseling regarding risk of post-operative verbal memory decline.
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: Laboratory testing does not diagnose focal epilepsy; it addresses a provoked seizure or a metabolic mimic when one is suspected.

red_herrings.data_point: Independent right temporal polymorphic delta slowing on routine EEG and outpatient EEG report of 'bilateral temporal sharp transients of uncertain significance'
red_herrings.intended_effect: Conclude bitemporal or non-lateralized epilepsy, withhold surgical evaluation or pursue invasive monitoring prematurely before adequate non-invasive localization.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Right temporal polymorphic delta is a non-ictal propagated or independent non-epileptic finding; video-EEG captures 17 events with exclusive left anterior temporal ictal onset, establishing unambiguous left lateralization.

red_herrings.data_point: Normal prolactin level (11.4 ng/mL) documented in initial labs
red_herrings.intended_effect: Interpret normal prolactin as evidence of psychogenic non-epileptic events rather than true seizures, leading to misdiagnosis of PNES and inappropriate psychiatric referral.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Prolactin was drawn approximately 3 hours after the witnessed event — well outside the 10-20 minute post-ictal diagnostic window. A normal prolactin at this interval has no discriminatory value; it does not exclude a prior seizure.

red_herrings.data_point: Low-normal lamotrigine level (3.2 mcg/mL; reference 3.0-14.0 mcg/mL)
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute breakthrough seizures solely to non-adherence to lamotrigine therapy, missing the pharmacokinetic interaction and the need for a structural/surgical evaluation.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Carbamazepine co-administration induces UGT1A4-mediated glucuronidation of lamotrigine, reducing plasma concentrations by 40-70%. The low-normal lamotrigine level at 200 mg BID dosing in the presence of carbamazepine is a predictable pharmacokinetic interaction, not evidence of non-adherence; drug-resistance criteria are met based on prior AED trial failures, not AED levels alone.

metadata.real_seed_note: Clinical case seeded from open-access CC-BY cohort study of drug-resistant TLE with FCD Type IIIa dual pathology (Frontiers in Neurology 2020; PMID 33362691; PMC7758315). Patient details (demographics, HPI, AED history, EEG/MRI specifics) are independently authored and do not reproduce verbatim text from the source; the seed establishes the clinical phenotype of drug-resistant temporal epilepsy with confirmed dual pathology and surgical evaluation.
metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: drug-resistant left temporal epilepsy with three embedded distractors — (1) bilateral temporal EEG slowing creating false concern for bitemporal epilepsy; (2) normal prolactin drawn hours post-event misleading toward PNES; (3) low-normal lamotrigine level attributable to carbamazepine pharmacokinetic interaction rather than non-adherence. Dual pathology (HS + FCD IIIa) is not visible on prior 1.5T standard MRI and is only characterized on 3T dedicated epilepsy protocol, with major implications for surgical planning.
metadata.revision_reason: clinical tool review: interpret_labs demoted to optional in the case, which is where the tier is scored — the panel had been changed alone
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Six required tools including video-EEG and 3T epilepsy protocol MRI; three grounded red herrings (bilateral EEG slowing, delayed prolactin, enzyme-induction lamotrigine level); dual pathology (HS + FCD IIIa) identified only on 3T protocol; surgical evaluation pathway with FDG-PET and neuropsych battery.
